'''Peter Michael Rosenthal''' (June 1, 1941 – May 25, 2024) was an American-Canadian mathematician, lawyer, and activist who was Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Toronto]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.toronto.edu/cms/rosenthal-peter/ |title=Rosenthal, Peter |website=Department of Mathematics |publisher=University of Toronto |date= |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref> and an adjunct professor of law at the [[University of Toronto Law School]].<ref name=UTorontoAdjunct>{{cite web|url=http://www.law.utoronto.ca/faculty-staff/adjunct-visiting-faculty/peter-rosenthal |title=Peter Rosenthal |website=Faculty of Law |publisher=University of Toronto |date= |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.law.utoronto.ca/news/article-makin-peter-rosenthal-profile |title= Makin - Peter Rosenthal Profile |website=Faculty of Law |publisher=University of Toronto |date=2007-03-20 |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref>

== Early life and family ==
Rosenthal grew up in a Jewish family in [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]], [[Queens]], New York with his parents, Harold (1913–1983) and Esther (1914–1985), and two younger brothers, Erik and Walter.<ref name="Lorinc"/><ref name="fam">{{cite web |title=Overview of family history (with links to selected documents) 1. HAROLD, IRVING, & SANDY ROSENTHAL AND THEIR PARENTS, ALBERT & NAOMI |url=http://probability.ca/harold-rosenthal/rosenthal-overview.html |access-date=May 28, 2024}}</ref> Rosenthal described himself as a "[[red diaper baby]]".<ref name=TheStar2014/> His father was a high school math teacher and his mother was a left-wing activist<ref name=TheStar2014/> who had been a member of the [[Communist Party USA|Communist Party]] in her youth.<ref name="Queens">{{cite web |title=Wally Rosenthal Oral History |url=https://queenslibrary.aviaryplatform.com/collections/21/collection_resources/4565?embed=true |publisher=Queens Public Library |access-date=August 25, 2024}}</ref>

His maternal grandmother, Sonia, had immigrated to New York from Russia after the failed [[1905 Russian Revolution]]  and was a supporter of the [[Bolshevik]]s.<ref name="cjn"/>

Rosenthal himself was also a committed activist and in 1960 participated in protests at the [[F. W. Woolworth Company|Woolworth]]'s in Flushing in solidarity with the [[Greensboro sit-ins|sit-ins at Woolworth's in Greensboro, North Carolina]] protesting racial segregation.<ref name="Queens"/>

Rosenthal had poor grades in high school and barely graduated, but after nearly failing in college due to the time he spent attending [[civil rights]] and [[anti-nuclear]] protests, he began to focus on his studies at [[Queens College, City University of New York|Queens College]], excelling in math.<ref name=TheStar2014>{{cite web |url=https://www.thestar.com/news/crime/2014/01/05/peter_rosenthals_passions_for_law_and_math_make_for_a_beautiful_if_different_life.html |title=Peter Rosenthal's passions for law and math make for a beautiful, if different, life |publisher=The Toronto Star |date=2014-01-05 |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref>

Erik Rosenthal is an emeritus professor of mathematics at the [[University of New Haven]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Erik Rosenthal, Ph.D. | url=https://www.newhaven.edu/faculty-staff-profiles/erik-rosenthal.php }}</ref> Their youngest brother, Walter (Wally) Rosenthal, is a community activist and trade unionist in [[New York City]] who taught at [[York College, City University of New York|York College]] after retiring from the [[United States Postal Service]]. Both Erik and Wally were civil rights and anti-war activists in the 1960s.<ref>http://digitalarchives.queenslibrary.org/browse/wally-rosenthal-full-interview</ref>

== Mathematics career ==
Rosenthal graduated from [[Queens College, City University of New York]] with a B.S. in mathematics in 1962.<ref name=MAAprofile>{{cite web|url=http://www.maa.org/careers/career-profiles/law/peter-rosenthal |title=Peter Rosenthal |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |date= |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref> In 1963 he obtained an MA in Mathematics and in 1967 a Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[University of Michigan]];<ref name=MAAprofile /> his Ph.D. thesis advisor was [[Paul Halmos]].<ref name=MathGenealogy>{{cite web|url=http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=5483 |title=Peter Rosenthal |website=The Mathematics Genealogy Project |date= |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref> His thesis, "On lattices of invariant subspaces"<ref name=MathGenealogy /> concerns operators on [[Hilbert space]], and most of his subsequent research was in operator theory and related fields. Much of his work was related to the [[invariant subspace problem]], the still-unsolved problem of the existence of invariant subspaces for bounded linear operators on Hilbert space. He made substantial contributions to the development of reflexive and reductive operator algebras and to the study of lattices of invariant subspaces, composition operators on the Hardy-Hilbert space and linear operator equations.  His publications include many with his long-time collaborator Heydar Radjavi,<ref name=TheStar2014 /> including the book ''Invariant Subspaces'' (Springer-Verlag, 1973; second edition 2003).

In 1967, Rosenthal moved to Canada to accept an assistant professorship at the [[University of Toronto]] where he remained for the rest of his career, eventually becoming a full professor and retiring as a [[professor emeritus]].<ref name="Helen"/>

Rosenthal supervised the Ph.D. theses of fifteen students<ref name=MathGenealogy /> and the research work of a number of post-doctoral fellows.

== Legal career ==
In parallel with his career in mathematics, Rosenthal pursued a career in law.  While teaching at the [[University of Toronto]] in 1969, Rosenthal was arrested while giving a speech at an [[Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War|anti-Vietnam War]] demonstration outside of the US [[consulate]] in [[Toronto]].<ref name=TheStar2014/> Representing himself in court, he was acquitted of obstructing police but convicted of causing a disturbance, but was able to have his conviction overturned on appeal. With his newfound interest in the law, Rosenthal began volunteering as a paralegal representing friends and activists who had been arrested and charged with minor criminal offences at protests or for [[civil disobedience]] or other activist-related offences, particularly related to [[civil rights]] or [[anti-racist]] activity.<ref name="left"/><ref name="Lorinc"/> Rosenthal was threatened by the [[Law Society of Upper Canada]] for practicing law without a license and he hired [[Charles Roach]] to represent him before the law society. The law society abandoned its action after Roach moved a motion to move the disciplinary proceeding to court.<ref name=TheStar2014/>

In the 1980s, Rosenthal worked with Roach representing 21 peace activists who had been charged in relation to protests against [[Litton Industries]] and their work on manufacturing components for [[cruise missiles]], with Rosenthal arguing that Litton executives were endangering the safety of Canadians through its products.<ref name="Lorinc"/> Rosenthal was also involved in a campaign to protest an invitation to [[South Africa]] ambassador [[Glenn Babb]] to speak at the [[University of Toronto]] in defence of South African's [[apartheid]] regime. Rosenthal was one of four University of Toronto professors who sought an [[injunction]] to stop Babb along with a declaration by the court that apartheid was a [[crime against humanity]]. While this effort was unsuccessful it helped lead to a later decision by the university to [[Disinvestment from South Africa|divest from South Africa]].<ref name="Lorinc"/>

Roach encouraged Rosenthal to go  to law school so that he could represent clients in more serious cases, and he was admitted to [[University of Toronto Law School]] in 1987 at the age of 46.<ref name="TL"/><ref name=TheStar2014/> He went on to obtain an LL.B. in 1990 and was called to the Ontario [[Bar (law)|bar]] in 1992.<ref name=UTorontoAdjunct />  Rosenthal joined Roach's firm as a partner.<ref name="Lorinc"/>

He was a major figure in the Toronto legal community, and was profiled by ''[[Toronto Life]]'',<ref name="TL">{{cite web|url=http://www.torontolife.com/features/agitator |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120213215709/http://www.torontolife.com/features/agitator |title=The Agitator |publisher=torontolife.com |date=January 2008 |accessdate=2014-08-01 |archivedate=2012-02-13}}</ref> ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'',<ref name=GlobaAndMail>{{cite news|author=Kirk Makin |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/on-the-left-side-of-the-law/article1353831/ |title=On the left side of the law |work=The Globe and Mail |date= 3 March 2007|accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref>  and the [[Toronto Star]]<ref name=TheStar2014 />  In 2006, [[Now (newspaper)|''Now Magazine'']] named Rosenthal Toronto's "Best activist lawyer".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.law.utoronto.ca/news/peter-rosenthal-%C3%AD90-selected-%C3%ACbest-activist-lawyer%C3%AE |title=Peter Rosenthal selected Best Activist Lawyer |website=Faculty of Law |publisher=University of Toronto |date=2007-03-20 |accessdate=2014-08-01}}</ref> In May 2016, he was awarded a Law Society Medal by the Law Society of Upper Canada.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lsuc.on.ca/newsarchives.aspx?id=2147485737&cid=2147502321|title=Law Society Announces 2016 Award Recipients|website=www.lsuc.on.ca|access-date=2016-06-09}}</ref>

Rosenthal provided legal services for various leftist causes and marginalized clients for free. He was also active in civil law suing police and public officials,<ref name="left"/> and participated in [[inquest]]s into the police shootings of several Black men, representing the families of the deceased.<ref name="Lorinc"/>

Rosenthal represented [[Miguel Figueroa]], the leader of the [[Communist Party of Canada]], in the case [[Figueroa v. Canada (Attorney General)|Figueroa v. Canada]] before the [[Supreme Court of Canada]].<ref name=GlobaAndMail />  The court ruled in Figueroa's favor, striking down a law that prohibited small political parties from obtaining the same tax benefits as large parties.

Rosenthal represented many activists who faced charges as a result of political protests, including [[Shawn Brant]], [[John Clarke (activist)|John Clarke]] and the [[Ontario Coalition Against Poverty]], Vicki Monague of Stop Dump Site 41, [[Dudley Laws]] and the [[Black Action Defence Committee]], and [[Jaggi Singh (activist)|Jaggi Singh]] and others arrested at the [[2010 G20 Toronto summit protests]], and wrote articles about some of those cases.<ref>{{cite web|first=Peter |last=Rosenthal |year=2020 |title=Articles archived on Medium.com
|url=https://rosenthalpeter7.medium.com/}}</ref> In 2006, Rosenthal represented Indigenous activists at the [[Ipperwash Crisis]] and cross-examined former [[Premier of Ontario]] [[Mike Harris]] over allegedly saying ""I want the fucking Indians out of the park."<ref>{{cite news |title=Harris denies ever using profane slur against natives |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/harris-denies-ever-using-profane-slur-against-natives-1.592725 |work=CBC News |date=February 16, 2006}}</ref>

== Personal life and death ==
Rosenthal married his first wife, Helen Black (1942–2017), in 1960 when he was 19 and she was 18. Both of them were social activists and would become mathematicians at the University of Toronto.<ref name="Helen"/> They divorced in 1979, but remained friends.<ref name="Helen"/> Rosenthal married his second wife, Carol Kitai, a medical doctor, in 1985.<ref name=TheStar2014/>

Rosenthal was a lifelong [[Marxist]] and political activist. He was a [[red diaper baby]]; his mother was active in the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights]] and [[Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War|anti-war]] movements.<ref name=TheStar2014/><ref name="left"/> Rosenthal told the ''[[Globe and Mail]]'': "I regard myself as a Marxist, but not one affiliated with any particular parties... I have a very strong hatred of racism and the grotesque economic inequalities such as exist in the world. It is very deeply embedded in my bones."<ref name="left">{{cite news |title=On the left side of the law |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/on-the-left-side-of-the-law/article1353831/ |access-date=May 26, 2024 |work=Globe and Mail |date=March 3, 2007}}</ref>

Rosenthal died in Toronto on May 25, 2024, at the age of 82.<ref name="obit">{{cite news |title=Peter Rosenthal (death notice) |url=https://www.legacy.com/ca/obituaries/theglobeandmail/name/peter-rosenthal-obituary?id=55208238 |access-date=August 25, 2024 |work=Globe and Mail |date=May 29, 2024}}</ref> He had suffered from [[heart disease]] and [[Parkinson’s disease]], and died due to complications from [[COVID-19]].<ref name="Lorinc">{{cite news |last1=Lorinc |first1=John |title=U of T math professor Peter Rosenthal became a lawyer so he could take his activism to court |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-u-of-t-math-professor-peter-rosenthal-became-a-lawyer-so-he-could-take/ |access-date=June 5, 2024 |work=Globe and Mail |date=June 4, 2024}}</ref>

The song "A Little Rain (A Song for Pete)" (2016), by the alternative rock band the [[Arkells]], was inspired by Rosenthal. It was written by Arkells' lead singer Max Kerman, a friend of Rosenthal and his family.<ref name="cjn">{{cite news |last1=Ringel |first1=Heather |title=Obituary: Peter Rosenthal, 82, a Toronto professor and lawyer who saw the beauty in both exploring mathematics and representing social-justice activists |url=https://thecjn.ca/lives/obituaries/obituary-peter-rosenthal-82-a-uoft-professor-and-lawyer-who-saw-the-beauty-in-both-exploring-mathematics-and-representing-social-justice-activists/ |access-date=August 24, 2024 |work=Canadian Jewish News |date=June 10, 2024}}</ref>
